topics.title: How to play
topics.body:
Every mission starts in the **Mission** app. Read the briefing – it tells you what happened and what to look for.

Then go exploring. Use the **Terminal** if you want to type commands like a real hacker, or the **Files** app if you prefer to click around. Both show exactly the same computer.

Somewhere you will find a flag: a secret code that looks like `FLAG{...}`. Copy it into the Mission app to complete the mission.

Stuck? Each mission has three hints, from a gentle nudge to the exact answer. Hints cost a few points – but learning matters more than points.

topics.title: Hacking with permission
topics.body:
Ethical hackers – also called penetration testers – break into systems to find weaknesses before criminals do. The big difference: they always have **written permission** from the owner.

Breaking into a computer, account or network without permission is against the law, even if you only look around.

Everything in Hackdot is pretend: NovaTech is not a real company and nothing here touches a real computer. Practise as much as you like!

topics.title: Files, folders and paths
topics.body:
Files live in folders, and folders live in other folders. The very top folder is called the root and is written as `/`.

A path is the address of a file. An absolute path starts at the root, like `/var/log/syslog`. A relative path starts where you are right now, like `Documents/notes.txt`.

A few shortcuts: `~` is your home folder, `..` is the folder above the one you are in, and `.` is the folder you are in.

topics.title: Hidden files
topics.body:
On Linux, a file or folder whose name starts with a dot – like `.bashrc` – is hidden. A plain `ls` does not show it.

Hidden files are not secret or protected. They are hidden to keep folders tidy, which is exactly why attackers always look for them.

Use `ls -a` to see everything, or turn on **Show hidden files** in the Files app.

topics.title: Users and permissions
topics.body:
A computer can have many users. Each file belongs to one of them – its owner. The most powerful user is called `root`: the administrator, who can open everything.

`ls -l` shows permissions like `drwxr-xr-x`. The first letter is `d` for a folder or `-` for a file. Then come three groups of three letters: what the owner may do, what the group may do, and what everyone else may do. `r` = read, `w` = write, `x` = execute (for a folder: go into it). A `-` means not allowed.

If you try to open something you are not allowed to, you get `Permission denied`. Try `cat /root/top_secret.txt` to see it happen.

topics.title: Switching users and logging in
topics.body:
Sometimes the file you need belongs to another user. If you know that user's password, you can become them.

In the terminal, `su admin` switches to the user `admin` after asking for the password (the letters are not shown while you type). `exit` takes you back. `su - admin` also moves you to admin's home folder.

You can also switch for the whole computer: open the start menu, choose **Log out** and log in as someone else. Then the Terminal and the Files app both run as that user.

The list of users on a Linux computer is in `/etc/passwd`. Despite the name, it does not contain any passwords.

topics.title: Log files and searching
topics.body:
Computers write down what happens in log files, one event per line. On Linux they live in `/var/log`. Logs show who logged in, what failed and when – gold for anyone investigating an attack.

Logs can have thousands of lines, so nobody reads them from top to bottom. Use `grep` to show only the lines that contain the text you are looking for. Add `-i` to ignore upper and lower case, and `-n` to see line numbers.

topics.title: Pipes: combining commands
topics.body:
The pipe symbol `|` sends the output of one command into the next one, like water through a pipe.

`cat` prints a file, and `grep` filters lines – so `cat file | grep word` prints only the lines with that word. You can chain as many commands as you like.

topics.title: What is a flag?
topics.body:
In Capture The Flag (CTF) games, a flag is a piece of text that proves you solved a challenge. In Hackdot every flag looks like `FLAG{some_secret_text}`.

Flags often swap letters for numbers, like `p4ssw0rd`, so copy them carefully. Upper and lower case don't matter in Hackdot, but the `FLAG{` and `}` parts do.

Tip: keep track of anything interesting – passwords, file paths, ideas – in the **Notes** tab. Real hackers take notes all the time.

topics.title: Terminal tips
topics.body:
You don't have to type everything: tap the shortcut buttons above the keyboard. Buttons ending in `…` type the start of a command so you can finish it.

The ↑ button (or the up arrow key) brings back your previous commands.

If a name contains spaces, put it in quotes: `cat "my notes.txt"`.

Forgot how a command works? Type `help` followed by its name.
